sections.title: The Crisis of Expertise (PD)
sections.description:
In recent years, there has been intensive talk about a “crisis of expertise” unfolding in liberal-democratic societies. Along with suspicion toward established facts and institutional findings, techno-scientific experts – academic researchers, medical doctors, engineers, public health specialists – are widely seen as detached elites whose impartiality is questionable, and motivations can no longer be trusted. This concerning shift in public attitudes, the argument goes, has boosted the popularity of unverified and unregulated sources of knowledge (traditional healing practices, the wellness industry, social media influencers, self-tracking), and given rise to a dangerous “do your own research” (DYOR) culture that impedes our collective ability to distinguish sound advice from misinformation.
Drawing on classics in democratic theory, history of science, and the sociology of health and professions, as well as more recent work in STS and social-cultural anthropology, this course seeks to challenge the crisis narrative. Rather than treating expertise as a neutral measure of knowledgeability and competence, we will examine it as a social status granted by others, and as a site of ongoing, at times fraught, dialogue between belief systems, values, and ways of life. Through a series of case studies – debates around climate change, mandatory vaccination, environmental risk management, and mental health – we will see how certain actors come to be recognized as experts, while others are disqualified or disregarded; how boundaries between ‘science’ and ‘non-science’ are constructed and policed; and how sanctioned expertise often shapes policy decisions but also perennially becomes disputed and democratized. Readings include work by Steven Shapin, Ted Porter, Elena Conis, Andrew Abbott, Thomas F. Gieryn, Naomi Oreskes, Sheila Jasanoff, Brian Wynne, Steven Epstein, Shiv Visvanathan, Harry Collins, Michel Callon, Marion Fourcade, Gil Eyal, Owen Whooley, E. Summerson Carr, and Chris Kelty.
This is an SNF Paideia-designated course and is open to all Penn students, not only Paideia fellows.
